summary: This document defines key concepts of uncertainty and confidence for location information and outlines methods for handling location estimates that include uncertainty. It updates the definition of location objects (PIDF-LO) so the accuracy of a position can be stated.

eli5.summary: A location is rarely exact. This says how to say you are somewhere within this big circle, and how sure you are, rather than pretending to be at one point.

subtitle: Defines what uncertainty and confidence mean for a location estimate and adds a confidence element to PIDF-LO.

tldr.problem: A location estimate is never exact, but the PIDF-LO location format could carry uncertainty only with a fixed 95% confidence and had no way to say how sure the sender was or what the error distribution looked like.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines uncertainty and confidence in statistical terms, adds a confidence element with an optional pdf attribute to PIDF-LO, and gives methods for reducing, scaling and comparing uncertain locations.
tldr.outcome: Senders can state the true confidence of an estimate, and receivers get shared rules for turning an uncertain location into a point or circle or testing it against a region. It updates RFCs 4119 and 5491 and deprecates terminology in RFC 3693.

facts.label: Default confidence
facts.value: 95% when no confidence element is present

today: RFC 7459 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3693, RFC 4119 and RFC 5491.

sections.title: Why Uncertainty Needs a Standard
sections.content:
Location information is an estimate of where a Target is. Many factors add errors to the measurements behind it. How measurements are combined into an estimate is outside the IETF's scope, but the result travels in IETF formats, so this RFC says how uncertainty and its companion datum confidence are expressed and interpreted.

It provides a common nomenclature, describes methods to expand or reduce uncertainty to reach a required confidence, and describes methods to estimate the probability that a Target lies in a given region. These methods are simplified and meant for relatively small geographic areas. It also describes a confidence extension for the Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) of RFC 4119. The methods are statistical and meant for automatically determined location.
sections.eli5: A map pin that says 'about here' is more honest than one that pretends to be exact. This RFC is about saying how big 'about' is, and how sure you are.

sections.title: Uncertainty, Confidence and Distributions
sections.content:
Uncertainty comes from the limits of measurement and is most completely described by a probability distribution. A common simplification is a confidence interval: a central estimate plus an error range and a confidence. The confidence is an estimated upper bound on the probability that the true value lies within the range. The RFC's example is a length of 1.00742 +/- 0.0043 meters at 95% confidence. It says this does not assert that the value is 1.00742. Because these are statistical statements, asserting 100% confidence is rarely advisable.

Two distributions are considered. A normal PDF applies where many small random factors contribute to error, and its error range relates to the standard deviation. A rectangular PDF applies where errors are consistent across a limited range, such as one dominant rounding error, and is described by its half-width.

The RFC also fixes vocabulary. The terms precision and resolution from RFC 3693 are deprecated for quantitative use because they have many meanings in other fields. Accuracy is kept only as a qualitative word: an estimate with uncertainty X is more accurate than one with 2X at the same confidence, but nobody should say the accuracy is X.
sections.eli5: If you say 'my height is 150 cm, give or take 2, and I am 95% sure', you have given a guess, a wiggle room and how sure you are. All three are needed.

sections.title: Uncertainty in Location
sections.content:
A location estimate is specified in two or three dimensions, so its confidence interval is a region, called the region of uncertainty. The RFC assumes the Target is a single point in space. That is reasonable when the Target is small relative to the region, but not when the two are about the same size, as with a football stadium or a small country.

PIDF-LO can carry uncertainty using the shapes described in [GeoShape], but it carries no confidence. RFC 5491 fixes it at 95%, and PIDF-LO does not say what the distribution looks like. Missing uncertainty does not mean no uncertainty: it might not have been calculated or may be withheld for privacy. If only the Point shape is used, confidence and uncertainty are unknown, and a receiver can assume 0% confidence or infinite uncertainty.

Civic addresses are covered too. Every element that is absent is uncertain, and each present label selects a spatial partition, so the address is the intersection of those partitions. Removing elements raises uncertainty but does not raise confidence. DHCP location options from RFC 6225 have no confidence value, so 95% should be assumed.
sections.eli5: A civic address like 'King Street' is also a fuzzy answer: the fewer details you give, the bigger the area you could be in.

sections.title: The Confidence Element
sections.content:
A fixed confidence is preferred for consistency, but some existing systems use 38%, 67% or 90%. Without a way to say so, a location server must either rescale the region to reach 95%, degrading the data, or ignore the difference, giving a false impression of quality. A recipient that ignores the new element is no worse off than before.

The confidence element MAY be added to the location-info element of a PIDF-LO. It gives the confidence as a percentage, or the special value unknown when confidence is supported but not known. An optional pdf attribute takes unknown, normal or rectangular, and is only a claim that the distribution approximately fits that shape. If the element is absent, the confidence is 95% as in RFC 5491.

A confidence element MUST be included with all location information that has uncertainty, that is, every shape other than a Point, and MUST be omitted when only a Point is given. Generators SHOULD try to keep confidence equal in each dimension. Applications should be careful showing confidence other than 95%, because a subtle display such as fine shading may let a user miss a real difference in quality.

The RFC includes the XML schema and registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:conf and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:geopriv:conf with IANA.
sections.eli5: It is a small label on the location that says 'I am this sure' and, if known, what kind of guess it was.

sections.title: Working With Uncertain Locations
sections.content:
Calculations should be done in Cartesian space and converted back to latitude, longitude and altitude, never by treating latitude and longitude as flat axes. When rounding uncertainty, errors are rounded up and confidence is rounded down, so any manipulation loses some information.

  • Reduce to a point. Take the centroid of the region of uncertainty, which is the center for circles, spheres, ellipses and ellipsoids. The RFC gives a formula for the arc-band and a method for polygons and prisms. Reducing to a point loses information and may be misread as exact, so it should be done only where needed.
  • Convert to circle or sphere. Find the centroid, then use the longest distance from it to any point in the region as the radius. Confidence stays unchanged.
  • Drop altitude. Removing the vertical component turns a Sphere into a Circle, a Prism into a Polygon and an Ellipsoid into an Ellipse, and confidence can be raised using C[2d] >= C[3d]^(2/3). A Sphere at 95% becomes a Circle at 96.6%.
  • Scale uncertainty. For a rectangular distribution the region can only be shrunk, with Cr = Co * Ur / Uo. For a normal distribution it can grow or shrink using the inverse error function.
  • Test against a region. Assume rectangular uncertainty, scaled to 95%, and compute Pi = Co * Ao / Au, where Ao is the area of overlap. A probability of 50% or greater is recommended before deciding the Target is within the region.
sections.eli5: If you want a simple answer from a fuzzy blob, you can pick its middle, draw the smallest circle around it, or shrink it and be less sure. Each choice throws something away.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC works through several cases. Alice's ellipsoid reduces to its center point, to a sphere of radius 28.7 meters, or, with altitude dropped, to a circle of radius 7.7156 meters. Bob's polygon roughly matches the Sydney Opera House, covers about 12600 square meters, and becomes a circle of radius 99.1 meters.

For scaling, a 19% estimate with a normal distribution is scaled by a factor of 2.9937 to reach 95%. For Bob's polygon, which is assumed rectangular, shrinking to the Concert Hall area of 4566.2 square meters gives a confidence of 95% * 4566.2 / 12600 = 34%.

In the region test, a circle of 1950 meters radius is checked against Bob's estimate with an uncertainty radius of 7.7156 meters. The distance between centers is 1915.26 meters and the estimated probability that Bob is inside is 67.8%. With 1920 meters the probability falls to 49.8%, so it is marginally more likely Bob is outside, even though the center of his estimate is inside.
sections.eli5: Even if the middle of your pin is inside a park, you might be more likely to be outside it if the pin is close to the edge and the blob is big.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC finds no specific security concerns in most of its content, and the considerations of RFC 4119 all apply. Privacy is discussed in RFC 6280. Including uncertainty increases the information available, and altering uncertainty is not an effective privacy mechanism. Uncertainty and confidence can also reveal how the location was generated, for example hinting at a GPS-equipped mobile device or a particular network service. A Rule Maker might remove uncertainty fields to protect that, though obfuscation (see RFC 6772) may still not fully protect it.

Adding confidence risks misinterpretation by consumers that do not understand the element, particularly when confidence is reduced. The RFC judges the impact as low.
sections.eli5: Telling how fuzzy your location is can also tell someone how it was found. Making it fuzzier does not always hide you.
